question: On an anteroposterior radiograph of the clavicle, which labeled structure lies at the lateral articulation with the scapula?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Sternoclavicular joint
options.rationale: Incorrect because the sternoclavicular joint is at the medial end of the clavicle; if the medial end were asked, this would be correct.

options.text: Acromioclavicular joint
options.rationale: Correct because the lateral clavicular articulation with the scapula is the acromioclavicular joint, a labeled landmark on AP clavicle films.

options.text: Coracoid process
options.rationale: Incorrect because the coracoid process is a scapular projection near the shoulder but not the lateral clavicular articulation; it would be correct if the question asked for a scapular projection adjacent to the clavicle.

options.text: Greater tubercle
options.rationale: Incorrect because the greater tubercle is on the proximal humerus, not the lateral clavicle; it would be correct if the film centered on humeral landmarks.

options.text: Glenoid fossa
options.rationale: Incorrect because the glenoid fossa is the scapular socket for the humeral head and not the lateral clavicular articulation; it would be correct if asking about the scapulohumeral joint.

question: Which radiographic view is perpendicular to an anteroposterior shoulder film and commonly obtained to assess joint alignment?
cited_learning_objective: Define orthogonal radiographic views

options.text: Axillary view
options.rationale: Correct because the axillary view is orthogonal to the AP shoulder and is described as an orthogonal view to assess humeral head–glenoid relationships.

options.text: Oblique lumbar view
options.rationale: Incorrect because an oblique lumbar view is a spine projection unrelated to shoulder orthogonality; it would be correct only if the question targeted lumbar spine imaging.

options.text: AP pelvis view
options.rationale: Incorrect because AP pelvis is not perpendicular to AP shoulder; it would be correct if the question asked about pelvic imaging.

options.text: Frog leg lateral hip
options.rationale: Incorrect because the frog leg lateral is a hip projection and not an orthogonal partner to AP shoulder; it would be correct for hip orthogonality.

options.text: Wrist PA view
options.rationale: Incorrect because a wrist PA is unrelated to shoulder imaging; it would be correct only if the question concerned wrist projections.

question: A child’s AP pelvis radiograph shows radiolucent lines at the ends of long bones. These lines represent which anatomic region?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Epiphyseal plates
options.rationale: Correct because pediatric pelvic and long bone films commonly show physes (epiphyseal plates) as radiolucent lines at bone ends, noted in the lecture.

options.text: Intertrochanteric lines
options.rationale: Incorrect because intertrochanteric lines are specific femoral landmarks, not the general radiolucent growth plates seen at multiple long bone ends; would be correct if the finding were limited to the proximal femur.

options.text: Subchondral sclerosis
options.rationale: Incorrect because subchondral sclerosis appears as increased density beneath joint cartilage, not radiolucent lines; it would be correct if increased density were described.

options.text: Metaphyseal cupping
options.rationale: Incorrect because metaphyseal cupping is a metaphyseal contour change, not the linear radiolucent physis; it would be correct if the radiograph showed metaphyseal deformity.

options.text: Periosteal reaction
options.rationale: Incorrect because periosteal reaction is new bone along the cortex, not the growth plate line; it would be correct if cortical elevation or layering were present.

question: On a lateral elbow film, which rounded structure articulates with the capitulum and is commonly fractured in adults after a fall onto an outstretched hand?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Radial head
options.rationale: Correct because the radial head articulates with the capitulum and is identified in the lecture as the most common adult elbow fracture from a fall on an outstretched hand.

options.text: Olecranon process
options.rationale: Incorrect because the olecranon is the proximal ulna projection forming the elbow tip; it would be correct if the fracture involved the posterior ulna.

options.text: Medial epicondyle
options.rationale: Incorrect because the medial epicondyle is a humeral prominence, not the rounded articulating structure with the capitulum; it would be correct if the question asked about epicondylar avulsion.

options.text: Coronoid process
options.rationale: Incorrect because the coronoid process is a ulnar eminence that articulates with the trochlea, not the capitulum; it would be correct if the trochlear articulation were described.

options.text: Lateral epicondyle
options.rationale: Incorrect because the lateral epicondyle is a humeral landmark adjacent to the capitulum but not the articulating rounded structure; it would be correct if the question targeted epicondylar anatomy.

question: Why should at least two perpendicular projections be obtained for most bone and joint radiographic exams?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.text: To reduce superimposition and increase fracture detection
options.rationale: Correct because orthogonal views reduce the effect of overlapping anatomy and improve sensitivity for fractures, as emphasized in the lecture.

options.text: To decrease radiation dose to the patient overall
options.rationale: Incorrect because obtaining additional views increases, not decreases, cumulative exposure; it would be correct only if fewer views could provide equivalent diagnostic information.

options.text: To visualize soft tissue contrast better than MRI
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films provide limited soft tissue detail compared with MRI; it would be correct only if the modality were MRI rather than radiography.

options.text: To eliminate the need for clinical correlation
options.rationale: Incorrect because radiographs do not replace clinical assessment; it would be correct only if imaging could fully substitute for clinical exam, which the lecture does not claim.

options.text: To ensure all growth plates are ossified on pediatric films
options.rationale: Incorrect because orthogonal views do not change ossification status; it would be correct only if the imaging timing, not projection, determined ossification visibility.

question: A toddler presents after twisting the leg; AP view is unremarkable but a lateral film shows a subtle cortical step in the tibia. What principle explains why the fracture was only seen on the lateral projection?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.text: Orthogonal views reveal fractures hidden by superimposed anatomy
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture demonstrates that perpendicular projections can reveal fractures obscured on a single view due to overlapping structures.

options.text: Lateral views always have higher spatial resolution
options.rationale: Incorrect because lateral views do not inherently have higher resolution; they simply present a different projection that may unmask displaced fragments.

options.text: AP views are contraindicated in pediatric trauma
options.rationale: Incorrect because AP views are not contraindicated; they are routinely obtained but may miss certain fracture orientations.

options.text: Fractures only become radiopaque on lateral films
options.rationale: Incorrect because fracture visibility depends on projection and displacement, not on becoming radiopaque on one view; it would be correct only if fracture mineralization changed between views.

options.text: Lateral projection reduces motion artifact compared with AP
options.rationale: Incorrect because motion artifact depends on patient movement, not projection; it would be correct only if the lateral film were obtained with better immobilization.

question: Identify the long bone region that is the narrow central shaft on an AP humerus radiograph.
cited_learning_objective: Recognize the epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis of a long bone on a radiograph

options.text: Diaphysis (shaft)
options.rationale: Correct because the diaphysis is defined in the lecture as the narrow central portion of a long bone and is visible on AP humerus films.

options.text: Proximal epiphysis
options.rationale: Incorrect because the proximal epiphysis is the rounded end forming part of the joint, not the central shaft; it would be correct if the question asked about the bone end.

options.text: Distal metaphysis
options.rationale: Incorrect because the distal metaphysis is the flaring region near the end, not the central shaft; it would be correct if the flared region were described.

options.text: Apophyseal plate
options.rationale: Incorrect because apophyses are secondary ossification centers and not the diaphyseal shaft; it would be correct if the question targeted secondary ossification.

options.text: Periosteal collar
options.rationale: Incorrect because the periosteal collar is a cortical feature, not the central diaphysis; it would be correct if cortical reaction were the focus.

question: A radiograph shows a fracture through the femoral neck in an elderly patient. Which named fracture type is this, and why is distinguishing it from an intertrochanteric break important on imaging?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Femoral neck fracture; location affects surgical approach
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists femoral neck and intertrochanteric fractures as distinct common hip fractures; the site influences management and fixation strategy.

options.text: Intertrochanteric fracture; it spares the femoral neck
options.rationale: Incorrect because an intertrochanteric fracture occurs between trochanters, not through the femoral neck; it would be correct only if the fracture line were between trochanters.

options.text: Subtrochanteric fracture; involves the femoral shaft
options.rationale: Incorrect because subtrochanteric fractures are distal to the trochanters in the shaft; it would be correct if the fracture were below the trochanters.

options.text: Acetabular fracture; involves the pelvic socket
options.rationale: Incorrect because acetabular fractures involve the pelvis, not the proximal femur; it would be correct if the radiograph showed pelvic disruption.

options.text: Greater trochanter avulsion; tendon insertion injury
options.rationale: Incorrect because greater trochanter avulsion is a localized trochanteric injury, not a femoral neck fracture; it would be correct if the fragment were at the trochanter.

question: Which term best describes a location on an appendage that is farther from the torso?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the meaning of the terms "proximal" and "distal" as applied to locations in the appendicular skeleton

options.text: Distal
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture defines distal as farther from the point of attachment of the appendage to the torso.

options.text: Proximal
options.rationale: Incorrect because proximal means closer to the torso; it would be correct if the location were nearer the point of attachment.

options.text: Medial
options.rationale: Incorrect because medial refers to toward the midline, not distance along the limb; it would be correct if the position were toward the body's midline.

options.text: Lateral
options.rationale: Incorrect because lateral denotes away from the midline, not distal versus proximal; it would be correct if the position were toward the side of the body.

options.text: Superficial
options.rationale: Incorrect because superficial refers to depth relative to the surface, not distance along the limb; it would be correct if the question asked about depth.

question: A patient with wrist pain has focal tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall. Which carpal bone is most likely injured based on that exam finding?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Scaphoid
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that focal tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is a sign of scaphoid fracture, the most frequently fractured carpal bone.

options.text: Lunate
options.rationale: Incorrect because lunate injuries present differently and are centrally located; it would be correct if central wrist collapse or dislocation were described.

options.text: Triquetrum
options.rationale: Incorrect because the triquetrum lies on the ulnar side and is less associated with snuffbox tenderness; it would be correct if ulnar-sided pain were the finding.

options.text: Pisiform
options.rationale: Incorrect because the pisiform is a palmar ulnar sesamoid and not typically tender in snuffbox injuries; it would be correct if palmar ulnar pain were present.

options.text: Hamate
options.rationale: Incorrect because hamate fractures classically cause ulnar-sided hand pain and are associated with hook injuries; it would be correct if the ulnar palm or hypothenar region were tender.

question: Which carpal series mnemonic corresponds to the proximal row from radial to ulnar on a PA wrist film?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists the proximal carpal row in that order on PA wrist films and provides the mnemonic for recall.

options.text: Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate
options.rationale: Incorrect because that sequence is the distal carpal row; it would be correct if the question asked for distal carpal order.

options.text: Capitate, Hamate, Scaphoid, Lunate
options.rationale: Incorrect because this mixes distal and proximal bones out of anatomical order; it would be correct only if the film orientation were reversed and bones relabeled.

options.text: Pisiform, Triquetrum, Lunate, Scaphoid
options.rationale: Incorrect because this reverses the proximal row order; it would be correct only if listing ulnar-to-radial rather than radial-to-ulnar.

options.text: Hamate, Capitate, Trapezoid, Trapezium
options.rationale: Incorrect because this is the distal row listed ulnar-to-radial; it would be correct only if the distal row in that direction were requested.

question: A patient falls and presents with a displaced patellar fragment best seen on the lateral knee film. Which imaging principle explains why the fragment is more conspicuous laterally?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.text: Orthogonal projection separates overlapping structures
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture emphasizes that orthogonal views reduce superimposition, making fragments more visible on one projection than another.

options.text: Lateral films always use higher kilovoltage
options.rationale: Incorrect because exposure technique varies and is not the reason fragments appear; it would be correct only if exposure differences caused visibility changes.

options.text: AP views are taken with the knee flexed
options.rationale: Incorrect because AP views are typically taken with the knee extended; it would be correct only if the AP technique described included flexion.

options.text: Patellar fragments are radiolucent on AP films
options.rationale: Incorrect because fragments are not radiolucent on AP films; they may be obscured by overlap rather than invisible due to radiolucency.

options.text: Lateral projection eliminates all motion artifact
options.rationale: Incorrect because projection does not inherently eliminate motion; it would be correct only if the lateral film were obtained with superior immobilization.

question: Which labeled region of a long bone flares between the shaft and the end and is commonly involved in pediatric growth-related changes on radiographs?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize the epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis of a long bone on a radiograph

options.text: Metaphysis
options.rationale: Correct because the metaphysis is the flaring portion between diaphysis and epiphysis and is highlighted in the lecture as a distinct radiographic region.

options.text: Diaphysis
options.rationale: Incorrect because the diaphysis is the central shaft, not the flaring region; it would be correct if the shaft were described.

options.text: Epiphysis
options.rationale: Incorrect because the epiphysis is the rounded end forming part of the joint, not the flaring metaphysis; it would be correct if the joint surface were the focus.

options.text: Periosteum
options.rationale: Incorrect because the periosteum is a soft tissue covering and not the metaphyseal flaring; it would be correct if cortical reactions were discussed.

options.text: Apophysis
options.rationale: Incorrect because apophyses are secondary ossification centers at tendon insertions, not the metaphyseal flaring; it would be correct if tendon insertion sites were in question.

question: A radiograph of the ankle shows a fracture of the lateral malleolus. Which bone is fractured?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Distal fibula
options.rationale: Correct because the lateral malleolus is the distal end of the fibula, as identified on AP and lateral ankle radiographs in the lecture.

options.text: Distal tibia
options.rationale: Incorrect because the distal tibia forms the medial malleolus, not the lateral; it would be correct if the medial malleolus were fractured.

options.text: Talus
options.rationale: Incorrect because the talus is an articular tarsal bone beneath the malleoli; it would be correct if the talar dome were fractured.

options.text: Calcaneus
options.rationale: Incorrect because the calcaneus is the heel bone and not the lateral malleolus; it would be correct if the heel were injured.

options.text: Navicular
options.rationale: Incorrect because the navicular is a midfoot bone on the medial side, not the lateral malleolus; it would be correct if medial midfoot pain were present.

question: Which imaging limitation of plain films explains why early bone infection or stress fractures may be missed on initial radiographs?
cited_learning_objective: Limitations of skeletal radiographs

options.text: Low sensitivity for early bone pathology
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists limited sensitivity for early tumor or infection and stress fractures as a limitation of plain films.

options.text: Excessive soft tissue contrast compared with CT
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films have limited soft tissue contrast, not excessive; it would be correct only if the modality provided superior soft tissue detail.

options.text: Inability to image cortical bone
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films do image cortical bone well; it would be correct only if cortical bone were radiolucent, which it is not.

options.text: Overestimation of fracture displacement
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films do not systematically overestimate displacement; it would be correct only if projectional magnification consistently exaggerated displacement.

options.text: Higher cost than MRI for initial screening
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films are less expensive than MRI; it would be correct only if MRI were cheaper, which contradicts the lecture.

question: A patient with suspected shoulder dislocation has an AP film showing loss of humeral head–glenoid contact. Which additional projection would best confirm the direction of displacement?
cited_learning_objective: Define orthogonal radiographic views

options.text: Axillary view to assess anterior versus posterior displacement
options.rationale: Correct because the axillary view is orthogonal to AP and helps determine anterior versus posterior shoulder dislocation, as described in the lecture.

options.text: AP pelvis to evaluate hip alignment
options.rationale: Incorrect because AP pelvis is unrelated to shoulder dislocation; it would be correct only if the hip were the joint of interest.

options.text: Lateral wrist to assess scaphoid alignment
options.rationale: Incorrect because lateral wrist views do not inform shoulder alignment; it would be correct only if wrist pathology were suspected.

options.text: Oblique lumbar spine to evaluate nerve roots
options.rationale: Incorrect because lumbar oblique views are unrelated to shoulder joint assessment; it would be correct only if lumbar pathology were present.

options.text: AP femur to visualize proximal femur
options.rationale: Incorrect because AP femur does not help shoulder dislocation evaluation; it would be correct only if the femur were being imaged.

question: Which carpal bone is most frequently fractured and should be suspected when snuffbox tenderness is present after wrist trauma?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Scaphoid
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explicitly states the scaphoid is the most frequently fractured carpal bone and associates it with snuffbox tenderness.

options.text: Lunate
options.rationale: Incorrect because the lunate is less commonly fractured and is centrally located; it would be correct only if central wrist collapse or dislocation were described.

options.text: Hamate
options.rationale: Incorrect because hamate fractures are less common and typically present with ulnar-sided hand pain; it would be correct if hypothenar pain were present.

options.text: Triquetrum
options.rationale: Incorrect because the triquetrum is not the most frequently fractured carpal bone; it would be correct only if ulnar-sided dorsal wrist tenderness were the finding.

options.text: Pisiform
options.rationale: Incorrect because the pisiform is a sesamoid and rarely the primary fractured carpal bone; it would be correct only if palmar ulnar pain localized to the pisiform were present.

question: A radiograph of the forearm shows the radial styloid process labeled laterally. Which bone contains this landmark?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Radius
options.rationale: Correct because the radial styloid process is a distal projection of the radius and is identified on AP forearm films in the lecture.

options.text: Ulna
options.rationale: Incorrect because the ulna bears the ulnar styloid, not the radial styloid; it would be correct if the ulnar styloid were asked.

options.text: Humerus
options.rationale: Incorrect because the humerus is proximal and does not have a radial styloid; it would be correct only if proximal arm landmarks were in question.

options.text: Scaphoid
options.rationale: Incorrect because the scaphoid is a carpal bone and not the source of the radial styloid; it would be correct only if carpal anatomy were asked.

options.text: Capitate
options.rationale: Incorrect because the capitate is a central carpal bone unrelated to the radial styloid; it would be correct only if central carpal anatomy were the focus.

question: Which of the following is a common limitation of plain skeletal radiographs that may necessitate MRI or CT for further evaluation?
cited_learning_objective: Limitations of skeletal radiographs

options.text: Poor soft tissue detail compared with cross-sectional imaging
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists limited soft tissue information as a limitation of plain films, often prompting MRI or CT for better sensitivity.

options.text: Excessive sensitivity for early marrow changes
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films have limited sensitivity for early marrow or soft tissue changes; it would be correct only if the modality were MRI.

options.text: Inability to image cortical bone at all
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films image cortical bone well; it would be correct only if cortical bone were radiolucent, which is not the case.

options.text: Automatic detection of nondisplaced fractures
options.rationale: Incorrect because nondisplaced fractures may be missed on plain films; it would be correct only if the imaging modality had higher sensitivity.

options.text: Superior evaluation of soft tissues compared with ultrasound
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films are inferior to ultrasound for many soft tissue assessments; it would be correct only if comparing different modalities under specific conditions.

question: A patient’s AP femur film shows the greater trochanter laterally and the lesser trochanter medially. Which projection would best demonstrate the femoral neck fracture if suspected but not seen on AP?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Frog leg lateral hip projection to profile the femoral neck
options.rationale: Correct because the frog leg lateral (lateral hip) profiles the femoral neck and can reveal fractures not obvious on AP, as the lecture notes lateral hip views.

options.text: AP pelvis with both hips internally rotated
options.rationale: Incorrect because AP pelvis may not profile the femoral neck as well as a lateral hip; it would be correct only if internal rotation improved neck visualization and the fracture were aligned for AP detection.

options.text: Oblique ankle projection to visualize distal tibia
options.rationale: Incorrect because an oblique ankle view images the distal tibia, not the proximal femur; it would be correct only if the distal tibia were the suspected site.

options.text: Lateral wrist projection to assess scaphoid
options.rationale: Incorrect because lateral wrist views do not help femoral neck assessment; it would be correct only if wrist pathology were the concern.

options.text: AP knee projection with weight bearing
options.rationale: Incorrect because AP knee weight-bearing films evaluate the knee joint and not the proximal femur; it would be correct only if knee pathology were suspected.

question: A 7-year-old’s AP pelvis shows open physes. Which statement best explains the radiographic appearance of these growth plates?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Physes appear as radiolucent lines at bone ends
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture describes epiphyseal plates (physes) as radiolucent lines visible on pediatric radiographs.

options.text: Physes are radiopaque sclerotic bands
options.rationale: Incorrect because physes are radiolucent, not sclerotic; it would be correct only if the growth plate were pathologically ossified.

options.text: Physes are indistinguishable from cortical bone
options.rationale: Incorrect because physes have a distinct radiolucent appearance separate from cortex; it would be correct only if imaging resolution were insufficient.

options.text: Physes indicate healed fractures in children
options.rationale: Incorrect because physes are normal growth plates, not healed fractures; it would be correct only if the lines represented fracture callus.

options.text: Physes are only visible after skeletal maturity
options.rationale: Incorrect because physes are visible in children and close with maturity; it would be correct only if the patient were skeletally mature.

question: A patient with suspected scaphoid fracture has a normal initial PA wrist film but persistent snuffbox tenderness. According to radiographic principles in the lecture, what is the most appropriate next imaging step?
cited_learning_objective: Common uses of skeletal radiographs

options.text: Obtain additional orthogonal wrist views and repeat radiographs later
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture emphasizes obtaining orthogonal views and notes that nondisplaced fractures may be occult initially, warranting repeat or additional projections.

options.text: Conclude no fracture and discharge without follow up
options.rationale: Incorrect because a normal initial film does not exclude scaphoid fracture; it would be correct only if clinical exam were normal and no concern remained.

options.text: Immediately perform MRI without further radiographs
options.rationale: Incorrect because while MRI is more sensitive, the lecture suggests plain films and orthogonal views are first-line; MRI would be appropriate if radiographs and clinical concern persist.

options.text: Apply a cast and avoid any further imaging
options.rationale: Incorrect because immobilization may be used, but the lecture supports further orthogonal imaging or follow-up films rather than abandoning imaging entirely.

options.text: Order an AP pelvis to evaluate hip referred pain
options.rationale: Incorrect because hip imaging is unrelated to suspected scaphoid injury; it would be correct only if hip pathology were suspected.

question: Which labeled landmark on an AP knee film corresponds to the proximal tibial articular surface?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Tibial plateau
options.rationale: Correct because the tibial plateau comprises the proximal tibial articular surfaces and is identified on AP knee radiographs in the lecture.

options.text: Femoral condyle
options.rationale: Incorrect because femoral condyles are distal femoral structures articulating with the tibial plateau; it would be correct if the femoral articular surface were asked.

options.text: Patellar tendon insertion
options.rationale: Incorrect because the patellar tendon inserts on the tibial tuberosity, not the articular plateau; it would be correct if the tuberosity were the focus.

options.text: Fibular head
options.rationale: Incorrect because the fibular head is lateral and not the proximal tibial articular surface; it would be correct if lateral proximal fibula anatomy were queried.

options.text: Intercondylar eminence
options.rationale: Incorrect because the intercondylar eminence is a central tibial spine between plateaus, not the plateau surface itself; it would be correct if the central tibial spine were the landmark.

question: A lateral ankle film demonstrates the base of the fifth metatarsal fracture after inversion injury. Which mechanism and landmark pairing from the lecture best explains this common injury?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Avulsion at base of fifth metatarsal from peroneus brevis pull
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture identifies the base of the fifth metatarsal as a recognizable landmark; avulsion fractures there commonly follow inversion injuries and tendon pull.

options.text: Medial malleolus compression fracture from eversion
options.rationale: Incorrect because medial malleolus fractures result from eversion mechanisms, not the lateral fifth metatarsal avulsion; it would be correct if eversion injury were described.

options.text: Calcaneal compression fracture from axial load
options.rationale: Incorrect because calcaneal fractures follow axial loading, not lateral inversion; it would be correct if a fall from height with heel pain were the scenario.

options.text: Navicular stress fracture from chronic dorsiflexion
options.rationale: Incorrect because navicular stress fractures have different mechanism and location; it would be correct if chronic midfoot stress and dorsal pain were present.

options.text: Talus osteochondral lesion from ankle impaction
options.rationale: Incorrect because talar osteochondral lesions are intra-articular and not the base of fifth metatarsal; it would be correct if talar dome symptoms were described.

question: Which statement best summarizes the primary clinical uses of skeletal radiographs as described in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Common uses of skeletal radiographs

options.text: First-line trauma evaluation, arthritis, tumor, and infection assessment
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists these indications—trauma/fracture, arthritis, tumors, and infection—as common uses of skeletal radiographs.

options.text: Primary modality for detailed soft tissue tumor staging
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films provide limited soft tissue detail and are not primary for detailed tumor staging; it would be correct only if cross-sectional imaging were referenced.

options.text: Preferred method for early stress fracture detection
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films have limited sensitivity for early stress fractures; it would be correct only if advanced imaging were unavailable and late radiographic signs were present.

options.text: Superior to MRI for marrow pathology detection
options.rationale: Incorrect because MRI is more sensitive for marrow pathology; it would be correct only if MRI were contraindicated and radiographs showed late changes.

options.text: Routine screening tool for asymptomatic bone metastases
options.rationale: Incorrect because radiographs are not sensitive for early metastatic disease and are not ideal for routine screening; it would be correct only if lesions were large and radiographically apparent.

question: A trauma patient’s AP tibia/fibula film is negative but clinical swelling persists. According to the lecture, what is the most appropriate immediate imaging principle to apply?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.text: Obtain a lateral orthogonal view to evaluate for occult fracture
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture emphasizes obtaining at least two orthogonal views to increase sensitivity and may reveal fractures missed on a single projection.

options.text: Proceed directly to bone scan without further radiographs
options.rationale: Incorrect because the lecture supports additional radiographic projections first; bone scan would be considered later if radiographs remain inconclusive.

options.text: Assume soft tissue injury and avoid further imaging
options.rationale: Incorrect because persistent clinical concern warrants additional imaging; it would be correct only if clinical exam definitively excluded fracture.

options.text: Order AP pelvis to assess referred pain
options.rationale: Incorrect because AP pelvis does not evaluate the tibia/fibula; it would be correct only if pelvic pathology were suspected.

options.text: Immobilize and schedule outpatient MRI in several weeks
options.rationale: Incorrect because immediate orthogonal radiographs are the recommended next step per the lecture; MRI delay may miss timely diagnosis.

question: Which bony landmark on an AP shoulder film corresponds to the humeral articular surface that resembles a golf ball on a tee?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Humeral head
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture uses the analogy of the humeral head and glenoid as a golf ball on a tee, identifying the humeral head as the rounded articular surface.

options.text: Acromion
options.rationale: Incorrect because the acromion is a scapular process forming the roof of the shoulder, not the rounded humeral articular surface; it would be correct if the superior scapular process were asked.

options.text: Coracoid process
options.rationale: Incorrect because the coracoid is an anterior scapular projection, not the humeral head; it would be correct if anterior scapular anatomy were the focus.

options.text: Greater tubercle
options.rationale: Incorrect because the greater tubercle is a humeral prominence adjacent to the head, not the spherical articular surface; it would be correct if the question asked about rotator cuff attachment sites.

options.text: Glenoid rim
options.rationale: Incorrect because the glenoid rim is the scapular socket edge, not the humeral head; it would be correct if the socket rather than the ball were the target.

question: A lateral wrist film is difficult to interpret due to overlapping bones. Which lecture point explains why lateral wrist films are challenging?
cited_learning_objective: Limitations of skeletal radiographs

options.text: Multiple overlapping carpal bones complicate lateral interpretation
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that multiple overlapping bones make lateral wrist films challenging to interpret.

options.text: Lateral films always have motion blur compared with PA
options.rationale: Incorrect because motion blur is not inherent to lateral projection; it would be correct only if patient motion occurred during acquisition.

options.text: Carpal bones are radiolucent and invisible on lateral films
options.rationale: Incorrect because carpal bones are visible but overlap; it would be correct only if carpal bones were radiolucent, which they are not.

options.text: Lateral wrist views are contraindicated in trauma
options.rationale: Incorrect because lateral views are not contraindicated; they are often obtained but can be hard to interpret due to overlap.

options.text: Lateral projection eliminates the need for PA views
options.rationale: Incorrect because lateral views complement PA views rather than replace them; it would be correct only if lateral views alone provided all necessary information.

question: Which structure is best visualized on an axillary shoulder projection that complements the AP view?
cited_learning_objective: Define orthogonal radiographic views

options.text: Relationship of humeral head to glenoid
options.rationale: Correct because the axillary view demonstrates the humeral head–glenoid relationship orthogonally to the AP view, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Intercondylar eminence of the tibia
options.rationale: Incorrect because the intercondylar eminence is a tibial knee landmark unrelated to shoulder axillary views; it would be correct if knee imaging were the subject.

options.text: Scaphoid waist on PA wrist
options.rationale: Incorrect because scaphoid waist is evaluated on wrist views, not the shoulder axillary projection; it would be correct if wrist imaging were asked.

options.text: Femoral neck profile on AP pelvis
options.rationale: Incorrect because femoral neck is a hip landmark, not visualized on shoulder axillary views; it would be correct only if pelvic imaging were performed.

options.text: Calcaneal tuberosity on lateral foot
options.rationale: Incorrect because calcaneal tuberosity is a heel landmark unrelated to shoulder axillary imaging; it would be correct if foot radiographs were the focus.

question: A patient’s AP clavicle film shows widening at the acromioclavicular articulation with inferior displacement of the acromion. Which diagnosis does this most closely represent?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Acromioclavicular joint separation (dislocation)
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture describes AC joint separation with widened joint space and acromial displacement as a recognizable abnormality on AP clavicle films.

options.text: Sternoclavicular dislocation
options.rationale: Incorrect because sternoclavicular dislocation affects the medial clavicle, not the AC joint; it would be correct if medial clavicular displacement were present.

options.text: Clavicular midshaft fracture
options.rationale: Incorrect because a midshaft fracture shows cortical discontinuity rather than isolated AC joint widening; it would be correct if a midshaft cortical break were visible.

options.text: Glenohumeral dislocation
options.rationale: Incorrect because glenohumeral dislocation involves humeral head–glenoid alignment, not AC joint widening; it would be correct if humeral head displacement were seen.

options.text: Acromial stress reaction without joint widening
options.rationale: Incorrect because stress reaction lacks joint widening and displacement; it would be correct only if there were periosteal change without separation.

question: Which radiographic sign on an AP forearm film indicates the presence of epiphyseal plates in a pediatric patient?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Visible radiolucent lines at distal radius and ulna
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes epiphyseal plates appear as radiolucent lines at the distal radius and ulna on pediatric forearm films.

options.text: Diffuse cortical thickening along the shaft
options.rationale: Incorrect because cortical thickening is not a feature of open physes; it would be correct if periosteal reaction were present.

options.text: Sclerotic bands across the metaphysis
options.rationale: Incorrect because physes are radiolucent, not sclerotic; it would be correct only if pathological sclerosis were present.

options.text: Periarticular joint space narrowing
options.rationale: Incorrect because joint space narrowing is unrelated to growth plates; it would be correct if arthritic changes were described.

options.text: Osteolytic lesion in the diaphysis
options.rationale: Incorrect because an osteolytic diaphyseal lesion is pathological and not the normal appearance of physes; it would be correct only if a lesion were present.

question: A patient presents after a fall with suspected shoulder anterior dislocation. The AP film shows the humeral head displaced inferiorly and medially relative to the glenoid. Which clinical next step aligns with the lecture’s imaging principles?
cited_learning_objective: Define orthogonal radiographic views

options.text: Obtain an axillary orthogonal view to confirm displacement direction
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture recommends orthogonal views (e.g., axillary) to assess humeral head–glenoid relationships and confirm dislocation direction.

options.text: Proceed to immediate MRI for rotator cuff evaluation
options.rationale: Incorrect because MRI is not the immediate next imaging step for confirming dislocation direction; it would be correct if soft tissue injury assessment were the primary concern after reduction.

options.text: Ignore imaging and attempt closed reduction without further assessment
options.rationale: Incorrect because orthogonal imaging helps guide management and should be obtained; it would be correct only if imaging were impossible and clinical judgment strongly favored immediate reduction.

options.text: Order AP pelvis to rule out referred hip injury
options.rationale: Incorrect because AP pelvis is unrelated to shoulder dislocation management; it would be correct only if hip injury were suspected.

options.text: Apply a short arm cast and discharge with analgesia
options.rationale: Incorrect because immobilization without confirming dislocation direction and planning reduction is inadequate; it would be correct only if no dislocation were present.

question: Which of the following best explains why nondisplaced fractures may be occult on initial plain films?
cited_learning_objective: Limitations of skeletal radiographs

options.text: Lack of cortical discontinuity and superimposition hide subtle lines
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that nondisplaced fractures may not be visualized due to superimposed anatomy and minimal cortical disruption.

options.text: Nondisplaced fractures are radiopaque and blend with cortex
options.rationale: Incorrect because fractures are not radiopaque; they may be radiolucent or subtle and are hidden by overlap, not increased density.

options.text: Plain films always detect all cortical breaks
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films have limited sensitivity and can miss nondisplaced fractures; it would be correct only if imaging sensitivity were perfect.

options.text: Nondisplaced fractures only occur in cancellous bone
options.rationale: Incorrect because nondisplaced fractures can occur in cortical or cancellous bone; it would be correct only if the pathology were restricted to cancellous bone.

options.text: Fractures are masked by increased soft tissue contrast on radiographs
options.rationale: Incorrect because soft tissue contrast is limited on radiographs and does not mask fractures in that manner; it would be correct only if soft tissue opacity obscured cortical lines.

question: A patient’s hand radiographs include PA, oblique, and lateral views. Which projection set is standard for foot radiographs as described in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: AP, oblique, and lateral foot views
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists AP, oblique, and lateral as standard radiographic views of the foot.

options.text: PA, frog leg lateral, and axillary views
options.rationale: Incorrect because frog leg lateral and axillary views are hip and shoulder projections, not standard foot views; it would be correct only if imaging those joints.

options.text: AP pelvis, AP femur, and AP knee
options.rationale: Incorrect because these are lower extremity but not the standard foot series; it would be correct only if imaging the entire limb.

options.text: Sunrise patellar, mortise ankle, and scaphoid view
options.rationale: Incorrect because these are specialized views for patella, ankle, and scaphoid, not the routine foot series; it would be correct if those specific regions were targeted.

options.text: Oblique wrist, lateral wrist, and PA wrist
options.rationale: Incorrect because these are wrist projections, not foot views; it would be correct only if the wrist were the area of interest.

question: Which radiographic landmark on an AP pelvis film corresponds to the articulation between the ilium and sacrum?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Sacroiliac joint
options.rationale: Correct because the sacroiliac joint is the ilium–sacrum articulation and is labeled on AP pelvis radiographs in the lecture.

options.text: Pubic symphysis
options.rationale: Incorrect because the pubic symphysis is the anterior pelvic midline joint, not the ilium–sacrum articulation; it would be correct if the anterior pelvis were asked.

options.text: Acetabulum
options.rationale: Incorrect because the acetabulum is the hip socket for the femoral head, not the ilium–sacrum joint; it would be correct if hip articulation were the focus.

options.text: Iliac crest
options.rationale: Incorrect because the iliac crest is the superior ilium margin, not the sacroiliac articulation; it would be correct if the superior pelvic rim were the landmark.

options.text: Ischial tuberosity
options.rationale: Incorrect because the ischial tuberosity is the inferior posterior pelvic prominence, not the sacroiliac joint; it would be correct if sitting surface anatomy were queried.

question: A lateral foot film shows a displaced calcaneal fracture after a fall from height. Given the lecture’s discussion of plain film limitations, which additional imaging modality is most likely to provide better detail of fracture extent if needed?
cited_learning_objective: Limitations of skeletal radiographs

options.text: CT for detailed bony architecture and fracture mapping
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that CT is often more sensitive than plain films for complex bony anatomy and can better delineate fracture patterns when plain films are limited.

options.text: Ultrasound for marrow edema assessment
options.rationale: Incorrect because ultrasound does not assess marrow edema well; it would be correct only if soft tissue or superficial tendon evaluation were the goal.

options.text: Plain radiographs repeated immediately without change
options.rationale: Incorrect because repeating identical plain films without different projections is unlikely to add detail; it would be correct only if a different projection were obtained.

options.text: DEXA scan for bone mineral density at the fracture site
options.rationale: Incorrect because DEXA measures bone density and is not used for acute fracture mapping; it would be correct only for osteoporosis assessment, not acute fracture detail.

options.text: Fluoroscopy for static marrow imaging
options.rationale: Incorrect because fluoroscopy provides dynamic real-time imaging but not superior static bony detail compared with CT; it would be correct only for procedural guidance.

question: Which of the following best describes the surgical neck location on an AP humerus radiograph?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize and correlate skeletal anatomy on plain films

options.text: Region distal to the humeral head and proximal to the shaft
options.rationale: Correct because the surgical neck is the constricted area just distal to the humeral head and proximal to the diaphysis, as labeled on AP humerus films in the lecture.

options.text: Distal articular surface of the ulna
options.rationale: Incorrect because this describes an ulnar distal landmark, not the humeral surgical neck; it would be correct if the ulna were the focus.

options.text: Insertion site of the rotator cuff tendons
options.rationale: Incorrect because rotator cuff tendons insert on the greater and lesser tubercles, not the surgical neck; it would be correct if tubercular anatomy were asked.

options.text: Proximal femoral neck adjacent to the trochanters
options.rationale: Incorrect because this describes hip anatomy, not the humeral surgical neck; it would be correct only if the femur were imaged.

options.text: Medial epicondyle projection at the distal humerus
options.rationale: Incorrect because the medial epicondyle is distal humerus, not the surgical neck; it would be correct if distal humeral landmarks were requested.

question: A patient with knee trauma has both AP and lateral films. The lateral shows a displaced patellar fragment while the AP is equivocal. According to the lecture, what does this illustrate about radiographic technique?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.text: Orthogonal views increase diagnostic sensitivity for fractures
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture uses the patellar fracture example to illustrate that orthogonal views can reveal fractures not obvious on a single projection.

options.text: AP views are sufficient for all knee fractures
options.rationale: Incorrect because AP views alone may miss fractures that are better seen on lateral projections; it would be correct only if all fractures were visible on AP.

options.text: Lateral views are unnecessary if AP is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect because the lecture advises obtaining orthogonal views even when one view appears normal; it would be correct only if clinical suspicion were absent.

options.text: Fractures are always more obvious on AP than lateral
options.rationale: Incorrect because visibility depends on fracture orientation; it would be correct only if fracture orientation favored AP projection.

options.text: Patellar fractures cannot be seen on radiographs
options.rationale: Incorrect because patellar fractures are often visible, particularly on lateral views; it would be correct only if radiographs were universally insensitive to patellar fractures.

question: Which of the following is the best single-sentence definition of an orthogonal radiographic view as used in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Define orthogonal radiographic views

options.text: A projection taken perpendicular to another projection
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture defines orthogonal views as projections perpendicular to one another, such as AP and lateral.

options.text: A projection taken at a 45-degree oblique to the body
options.rationale: Incorrect because orthogonal implies perpendicular, not oblique; it would be correct only if the view were specifically oblique.

options.text: A projection that always uses lower radiation dose
options.rationale: Incorrect because orthogonality refers to geometry, not dose; it would be correct only if dose considerations were specified.

options.text: A projection that images only soft tissues
options.rationale: Incorrect because orthogonal views image bone and soft tissue depending on projection; it would be correct only if soft tissue imaging were the goal.

options.text: A projection that replaces the need for clinical exam
options.rationale: Incorrect because imaging complements but does not replace clinical assessment; it would be correct only if imaging could fully substitute for clinical evaluation.

question: A pediatric AP pelvis shows both iliac crests and open physes. Which statement about pediatric skeletal radiographs is supported by the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Skeletal radiographs of pediatric patients often show epiphyseal plates

options.text: Epiphyseal plates are commonly visible on pediatric films
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explicitly states that pediatric radiographs often show epiphyseal plates (physes) and provides example images.

options.text: Epiphyseal plates are absent in children
options.rationale: Incorrect because physes are present in growing children; it would be correct only if the patient were skeletally mature.

options.text: Pediatric films never require orthogonal views
options.rationale: Incorrect because orthogonal views are recommended in nearly all cases regardless of age; it would be correct only if a specific exception applied.

options.text: Growth plates appear as dense sclerotic lines
options.rationale: Incorrect because growth plates are radiolucent lines, not sclerotic; it would be correct only if pathological ossification occurred.

options.text: Pediatric radiographs are superior to MRI for soft tissue
options.rationale: Incorrect because plain films have limited soft tissue detail compared with MRI; it would be correct only if MRI were unavailable and soft tissue detail were not required.

question: Which of the following best describes the metaphysis on a long bone radiograph?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize the epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis of a long bone on a radiograph

options.text: The flaring region between diaphysis and epiphysis
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture defines the metaphysis as the flaring portion between the shaft (diaphysis) and the end (epiphysis).

options.text: The narrow central shaft of the bone
options.rationale: Incorrect because that describes the diaphysis, not the metaphysis; it would be correct if the shaft were the target.

options.text: The rounded articular end of the bone
options.rationale: Incorrect because that describes the epiphysis, not the metaphysis; it would be correct if the joint surface were asked.

options.text: A tendon insertion site only in adults
options.rationale: Incorrect because apophyses are tendon insertion sites and not synonymous with metaphysis; it would be correct only if tendon insertion anatomy were specified.

options.text: A radiographic artifact from improper exposure
options.rationale: Incorrect because metaphysis is an anatomical region, not an imaging artifact; it would be correct only if the finding were due to exposure error.

question: A patient with suspected scaphoid fracture has persistent clinical signs but normal initial radiographs. Which management step aligns with the lecture’s guidance on limitations and next steps?
cited_learning_objective: Limitations of skeletal radiographs

options.text: Immobilize and obtain repeat radiographs or additional views
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that nondisplaced fractures may be occult and recommends additional orthogonal views or repeat radiographs when clinical suspicion persists.

options.text: Discharge without immobilization if initial films are normal
options.rationale: Incorrect because normal initial films do not exclude occult fractures; it would be correct only if clinical exam were unequivocally normal.

options.text: Immediate bone biopsy to exclude infection
options.rationale: Incorrect because biopsy is not indicated for suspected occult scaphoid fracture; it would be correct only if infection were strongly suspected with supporting signs.

options.text: Order DEXA scan to evaluate bone density at the wrist
options.rationale: Incorrect because DEXA assesses bone density and is not useful for acute fracture diagnosis; it would be correct only for osteoporosis assessment.

options.text: Perform ultrasound to visualize scaphoid cortical disruption
options.rationale: Incorrect because ultrasound is not the standard for scaphoid cortical assessment; it would be correct only if ultrasound expertise and indications supported its use.

question: Which of the following best captures the lecture’s recommendation about the number of views needed for complex anatomic regions?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss why at least 2 orthogonal views should be obtained in nearly all bone and joint radiographic exams

options.text: Some complex areas require more than two views for adequate evaluation
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states that while two orthogonal views are generally required, some complex anatomies need more than two projections to evaluate fully.

options.text: Two views are always excessive and should be avoided
options.rationale: Incorrect because the lecture advocates at least two orthogonal views to improve sensitivity; it would be correct only if minimizing radiation were the sole priority.

options.text: Single AP view suffices for all skeletal exams
options.rationale: Incorrect because single views often miss pathology; it would be correct only in rare, well-justified circumstances.

options.text: Oblique views are never useful in skeletal imaging
options.rationale: Incorrect because oblique views can be useful and are part of standard series for some regions; it would be correct only if obliques were contraindicated.

options.text: Complex anatomy should be imaged only with MRI
options.rationale: Incorrect because while MRI may be more sensitive for some pathologies, the lecture emphasizes radiographs and additional projections as first-line for many evaluations.
